content: Hysteroscopy performed in an outpatient setting is considered the gold standard for evaluating the uterine cavity. To facilitate this procedure, the uterine cavity is distended using either gas, such as carbon dioxide, or liquid, such as saline. These media can be used at room temperature or warmed to body temperature. Both types of media have their own advantages and disadvantages. The purpose of this review was to compare the effectiveness, tolerability, and safety of carbon dioxide gas and saline liquid as uterine distension media during outpatient hysteroscopy. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared saline with carbon dioxide, as well as trials comparing saline at different temperatures. A total of 12 RCTs involving 1,946 women were included in the analysis. The quality of evidence ranged from very low to moderate, with limitations such as lack of blinding, imprecision, and inconsistency. When comparing saline to carbon dioxide, the analysis found no clinically significant difference in pain scores during the procedure. However, the quality of evidence for this finding was low. The difference in pain scores was small, translating to a range of 0.39 cm lower to 0.05 cm higher on a 10-cm visual analogue scale (VAS). There was insufficient evidence to determine whether saline reduced the proportion of procedures abandoned due to intense pain or the need for analgesia compared to carbon dioxide. However, saline was associated with fewer vasovagal reactions and fewer instances of shoulder-tip pain. Specifically, if 10% of women experience a vasovagal reaction with carbon dioxide, this rate would decrease to between 3% and 9% with saline. Similarly, the rate of shoulder-tip pain would decrease from 9% with carbon dioxide to between 1% and 5% with saline. There was no clear evidence to suggest a difference in the rate of endometrial bleeding between the two media, and no infections were reported in any of the studies. Saline may also result in fewer procedures with an unsatisfactory hysteroscopic view compared to carbon dioxide. Additionally, the duration of the procedure was generally shorter with saline in most studies. When comparing warm saline to room temperature saline, the use of warm saline may reduce pain scores during the procedure. However, the evidence was insufficient to determine differences in the proportion of procedures abandoned due to intense pain or the need for analgesia. There was no clinically significant difference in the duration of the procedure between warm and room temperature saline. No cases of infection were reported in either group, and no other adverse events or information on the quality of the hysteroscopic view were provided. In conclusion, the evidence was insufficient to demonstrate significant differences between the various uterine distension media in terms of patient tolerability, operator satisfaction, or procedure duration. However, saline was associated with fewer adverse events, such as shoulder-tip pain and vasovagal reactions, compared to carbon dioxide.
